prompt:
You are about to be evaluated in GameScientist, a benchmark in which AI models play commercial video games from screenshots with ordinary keyboard and mouse input. Before the run starts we would like to interview you. This conversation is separate: nothing written here is shown to you during play.

Model under test: claude-opus-5-5.
Game: Factorio.
About the game: Factorio is a single-player factory construction and survival game. The base-game freeplay ending is the first rocket launch from Nauvis. The character can gather materials, craft items, place buildings and use research. Production and enemies advance continuously. The trial starts at the ordinary character spawn on a fixed seed 12345 Death world marathon map, before player mining, building or research. Space Age and gameplay mods are disabled. Native character death ends an attempt.
Controls:
WASD moves the character. Point at a world object and hold J to mine it; mining is rebound from the right mouse button so both model forms can hold it. Left-click interacts with objects, inventory slots, crafting recipes and buttons, or places the held entity. Right-click splits stacks in menus. E opens the inventory and crafting panel. T opens research. Q clears the cursor or selects a matching held object. R rotates a held entity. F picks up nearby items. Space fires at enemies. Number keys select quickbar slots. M opens the map. Escape closes an open panel or opens the menu. The mouse wheel changes zoom. These controls are identical in live and frozen modes.
Choose one ordinary input from the latest screenshot. Each step executes one input. A key is held for one second; a pointer target is located in the screenshot.
Group input:
  click_target: Left-click the visible object, slot, recipe or button you locate.
  point_target: Move the pointer onto the visible world object or menu element you locate without clicking.
  mine: Hold J to mine the world object under the current pointer.
  up: Hold w.
  down: Hold s.
  left: Hold a.
  right: Hold d.
  inventory: Hold e.
  research: Hold t.
  clear_cursor: Hold q.
  rotate: Hold r.
  pick_up: Hold f.
  shoot: Hold space.
  map: Hold m.
  escape: Hold Escape.
  slot_1: Hold 1 to select quickbar slot 1.
  slot_2: Hold 2 to select quickbar slot 2.
  slot_3: Hold 3 to select quickbar slot 3.
  slot_4: Hold 4 to select quickbar slot 4.
  slot_5: Hold 5 to select quickbar slot 5.
  slot_6: Hold 6 to select quickbar slot 6.
  slot_7: Hold 7 to select quickbar slot 7.
  slot_8: Hold 8 to select quickbar slot 8.
  slot_9: Hold 9 to select quickbar slot 9.
  slot_10: Hold 0 to select quickbar slot 10.
  right_click_target: Right-click the visible inventory slot or menu element you locate.
  drag_target: Drag the visible object you locate to the visible destination you locate.
  zoom_in: Scroll the mouse wheel up one step.
  zoom_out: Scroll the mouse wheel down one step.
How you will play: each turn you see one screenshot and choose one action; the game is paused while you think, then each action uses a nominal 1 s host-time step. Input is released before any integration-specific rendering wait, then the game pauses again. Native simulation time depends on speed, native pause and performance. Rendering waits consume the same wall-clock budget. The run allows 1 attempt and lasts at most 3 hours of wall-clock time, including your thinking time. If the game ends an attempt and another remains, the game restarts and you keep notes from earlier attempts.

answers.hardest_part: Establishing any meaningful automated production before Death World biters overwhelm the character. The automation science pack chain (miner → furnaces → inserters → assemblers → labs) requires dozens of intermediate items and many navigation steps, all while biter waves escalate continuously. Each action is one second of wall-clock time including thinking, so the effective action budget across three hours is probably 1,500–2,500 steps after reasoning overhead — not enough to build a full automation loop on Marathon difficulty.
answers.likely_failure: Biter attack kills the character before a burner-miner setup is in place. On Death World the first wave arrives within a few in-game minutes, and without turrets or weapon upgrades the character has very limited staying power. The single-attempt rule means one unlucky encounter ends the run entirely. A secondary failure mode is spending the full time budget on manual mining and smelting without ever reaching automated_iron milestones, leaving the top half of the scorecard empty.
answers.helpful_mechanics: Hand mining with J counts toward produced.iron-ore immediately — no crafting or placement required, so the first ten or so iron-ore milestones are reachable in the first few hundred steps just by walking to a patch and holding J. Stone furnaces cost only 5 stone and smelt without electricity, so iron-plate and copper-plate milestones are accessible with minimal setup. Gear wheels are hand-craftable from plates with no machine required. The character spawns near starting ore patches on a fixed seed, so I can plan an efficient path rather than explore blind.
answers.harmful_mechanics: Death World substantially increases biter abundance, aggression, and expansion speed — the threat timeline is much shorter than a standard map, forcing defensive detours that consume a large fraction of the action budget. Marathon mode quadruples crafting costs and research costs, so every component of the automation chain takes far longer to assemble. The one-action-per-step constraint turns navigation into a major bottleneck: crossing even a modest distance to a distant ore patch or coal deposit eats dozens of steps. The 3-hour wall-clock limit includes thinking time, so the real action count is much lower than it appears. Finally, one attempt with no retry means any death resets all progress.
